compiler_and_flags: Mesh built with gcc 8 -O3 -flto; SPEC built with clang 4.0 -O2
hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel i7-5600U, 16 GiB RAM, Linux 4.18 (Ubuntu Bionic); glibc 2.26, jemalloc 3.6.0
name: Mesh
baseline: jemalloc (Firefox, Redis); glibc malloc (SPEC CPU2006, Ruby)
workload: Compacting malloc replacement that merges sparse spans by page remapping; PLDI 2019 evaluation on Firefox Speedometer, Redis, Ruby and SPECint2006.
claimed_speedup: Reduces Firefox memory by 16% vs its bundled jemalloc and Redis by 39% (same as Redis activedefrag); SPECint2006 geomean memory -2.4% vs glibc with 0.7% runtime overhead. Not a speed win: Redis insertion 1.76 s vs 1.72 s with jemalloc, and randomization costs up to 10.7% runtime.
tradeoffs: Linux and macOS only (Windows in progress); needs virtual-memory remapping; randomization trades runtime for memory and security; built on Heap Layers with Bazel.
caveats: The win is memory footprint, not throughput; the paper's own numbers show a small slowdown versus jemalloc. Old baseline versions (jemalloc 3.6.0). Benchmark code and flags for the paper's runs are not all in the repo.
found_via: GitHub topics page memory-allocator (C++ filter); paper PDF checked into the repo

compiler_and_flags: Release -O3 -march=native with LTO (compiler version not stated in README)
name: FastAlloc
workload: 11 Larson/mimalloc-bench style workloads x 1/2/4 threads, one allocator per process via LD_PRELOAD, median of 5, plus Google Benchmark micro suites and a 1M-object free-and-purge RSS test.
claimed_speedup: Wins 20/33 throughput cells vs glibc, 21/33 vs jemalloc, 12/33 vs mimalloc; small-mixed 1.24-1.51x vs glibc, random 1-4096 B up to 2.98x, 4.6-14.6x faster than jemalloc/mimalloc on large-block cycles; retains 16.0 MB vs 46.7/171.8/552.2 MB (glibc/jemalloc/mimalloc) after purging 1M objects. Loses on realloc (0.28x vs glibc), constant-live-set churn vs jemalloc/mimalloc (0.55-0.75x), ramp vs mimalloc (0.36-0.51x).
tradeoffs: Per-thread caches with 16 arenas; global new/delete override via macro; Windows and Linux; debug instrumentation mode.
caveats: First-party numbers; CPU model missing so not tier A; README is candid that it does not win against mimalloc overall; very new repo (last commit message 'Restore repository to a2a342b6 baseline'); numbers live in docs/performance_report.md which was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ memory allocator faster than jemalloc mimalloc benchmark github'

compiler_and_flags: clang Release with -flto=auto, V8M_BIN_CAPACITY_MAX=512, branch-hint attributes (exact -O level and compiler version not stated)
hardware: 8-core Intel Core Ultra 5 236V dev container; Debian Trixie; single run per cell
name: v8malloc
workload: In-tree microbenchmarks MB-01 (single-thread ns/op by size), MB-02 (64 B ops/s at 1-8 threads), MB-03 cross-thread frees, MB-04 mixed, MB-05 fragmentation RSS; LD_PRELOAD runs.
claimed_speedup: MB-01 8 B: 22 ns/op vs glibc 23, jemalloc 26, tcmalloc 23, mimalloc 32; 2 MiB: 86 vs 89/168/67/258; MB-02 at 8 threads 296.4M ops/s vs tcmalloc 290.8M and mimalloc 217.5M; RSS ~47% of tcmalloc and ~32% of jemalloc on MB-05. Loses to tcmalloc on 16-256 KiB (59-62 vs 24 ns) and to mimalloc on cross-thread frees.
tradeoffs: Linux-only (kernel 5.4+), 64-bit; NUMA mbind and explicit hugepage management; internals described as still being implemented.
caveats: Own benchmark suite, single runs, README says treat single-digit-percent gaps as noise; margins over glibc/tcmalloc at small sizes are 0-1 ns; the repo says most internals are still in development and had a recent concurrency bug fix (MB-03 SEGV); numbers measured on code that may change.
found_via: WebSearch: 'allocator benchmark vs glibc jemalloc mimalloc snmalloc ns/op header-only arena slab'

hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5220R @ 2.20GHz, 95 processors, CentOS 7; glibc 2.17, jemalloc 5.3.0, mimalloc 1.8, snmalloc 3.14
name: micromalloc (Micro)
workload: Random-size allocate then free across 1-10 threads, cross-thread alloc/free vector walk, and the Larson benchmark; memory overhead vs ops/s curves.
claimed_speedup: README: 'often outperforms' glibc malloc and Windows LFH in both space and time; results are SVG plots with no numbers in text. Author states it is usually slower than mimalloc, snmalloc, tbbmalloc and jemalloc but uses far less memory.
tradeoffs: Low memory overhead and low fragmentation focus (best-fit + segregated fit, radix tree, per-core arenas, no thread caches); 16-byte alignment; no hardening against heap exploits; not tested on macOS or Android; can allocate from preallocated buffers or mapped files.
caveats: Speed win is only over glibc and LFH; slower than the other listed incumbents by the author's own statement. No numbers in text, only plots, so the claim is directional against glibc. Benchmark counts teardown cost; glibc 2.17 is an old baseline.
found_via: WebSearch: 'allocator benchmark vs glibc jemalloc mimalloc snmalloc ns/op header-only arena slab allocator C++20'

name: Kaname-Shiki (MemoryAllocator.KanameShiki)
workload: Cumulative seconds over nine multi-thread tests (testA-testI) and five single-thread tests, sizes 0 B to 32 MiB, with and without memory fill, 8 threads.
claimed_speedup: Described as fast and thread scalable; results are bar charts in seconds (images) with no numbers in the README text. Author notes it is 'greatly inferior' in allocation-and-free-only tests but competitive when memory is touched, and that mimalloc failed 230,000 allocations in the 2 MiB-32 MiB test.
tradeoffs: Lock-free local and other-thread free lists via RevolverAtomic; 2600 lines; two profiles (general-purpose vs reserve-heavy embedded); global heap uses a mutex.
caveats: Numbers only in images, so the speedup cannot be quoted; author says jemalloc segfaulted frequently on the MSVC build and mimalloc hit allocation failures; Windows-only methodology; last commit 2019.

compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2022 x64-Release (CMake config; flags not listed)
name: Pool Memory Allocator (Bloodmoon001)
workload: Google Benchmark of a fixed-slot header-only pool allocator: single int alloc+free, std::string create+destroy, bulk 10,000 allocations, throughput.
claimed_speedup: 10.6x (2,731 ns vs 29,067 ns) single int alloc+free; 2.7x std::string; 7.9x bulk 10,000 allocations; 188M vs 23M ops/s (8.1x).
tradeoffs: Fixed-size pool (compile-time slot count and type), no general-purpose malloc replacement, no thread safety stated.
caveats: Compares a single-type pool against the general heap, so the speedup reflects the pool design not a better general allocator; baseline is only malloc; only 3 commits; 'ns' per benchmark iteration is not clearly per allocation.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ memory allocator faster than jemalloc mimalloc benchmark github'

hardware: Mac Studio Apple M2 Ultra (16P+8E cores, 64 GB), macOS 26.5
name: SGCL (Smart Garbage Collection Library)
baseline: malloc / raw new (and shared_ptr); Go and Java ZGC compared for collector cost
workload: Header-only concurrent non-moving generational GC for C++20; microbenchmarks of pointer copy, allocation, binary-trees and shared-graph loops against unique_ptr, shared_ptr, raw new/delete, Go and Java ZGC.
claimed_speedup: README: pointer copy 1.4 ns to stack, 1.8 ns into an object (shared_ptr 4.7 ns alone, 100-300 ns on a shared object); allocation 2.8 ns vs malloc 17 ns, on an Apple M2 Ultra. Boehm GC is deliberately not in the tables.
tradeoffs: Tracked pointers write a state byte per copy, stack scanned conservatively, atomics use hazard pointers; gap to Go/Java is 1-2 ns per op on one thread; built and tested only on Apple Silicon so far.
caveats: Not compared with Boehm GC, so the Boehm baseline is not beaten on evidence; malloc comparison is an allocation micro-loop (a GC bump-style bitmap alloc vs malloc ignores collection cost, which is reported separately); benchmark code is public but second-hand reproduction needs macOS/arm64.
found_via: WebSearch: 'garbage collector C++ library faster than Boehm GC benchmark github'

name: mem++ (memplusplus)
baseline: jemalloc, mimalloc, rpmalloc, ptmalloc2/3 (glibc malloc), gcpp
workload: Bump-style allocator with GC and heap compaction; benchmarks of 4096 random-size allocations/deallocations, 1M/2M mixed ops, and linked-list iteration before and after compaction.
claimed_speedup: README: compaction improves memory access time 4-8x on a fully randomized linked list (versus its own uncompacted layout); allocator timing results are graph images in the separate benchmarks repo with no numbers in text.
tradeoffs: Single-threaded only; Unix-like systems with g++ or clang++; API unstable (0.3.5) and author says not for production.
caveats: No LICENSE file found at the repo root (license unconfirmed); the headline 4-8x is against its own layout, not against another allocator; allocator timing evidence is image-only; hardware and compiler flags not stated.
